original_value: We propose a new neural network called Temporal-enhanced Convolutional Network (T-CN) for video-based person reidentification. For each video sequence of a person, a spatial convolutional subnet is first applied to each frame for representing appearance information, and then a temporal convolutional subnet links small ranges of continuous frames to extract local motion information. Such spatial and temporal convolutions together construct our T-CN based representation. Finally, a recurrent network is utilized to further explore global dynamics, followed by temporal pooling to generate an overall feature vector for the whole sequence. In the training stage, a Siamese network architecture is adopted to jointly optimize all the components with losses covering both identification and verification. In the testing stage, our network generates an overall discriminative feature representation for each input video sequence (whose length may vary a lot) in a feed-forward way, and even a simple Euclidean distance based matching can generate good re-identification results. Experiments on the most widely used benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposal, in comparison with the state-of-the-art.

result.paraphrase: We introduce a new neural network for video-based person re-identification, called the Temporal-enhanced Convolutional Network (T-CN). For each person video sequence, a spatial convolutional subnet is first applied frame by frame to capture appearance information; next, a temporal convolutional subnet connects short spans of consecutive frames to extract local motion cues. Together, these spatial and temporal convolutions form the T-CN representation. A recurrent network is then used to further model global dynamics, followed by temporal pooling to produce a single feature vector for the entire sequence. During training, a Siamese architecture jointly optimizes all components with identification and verification losses. At test time, the network generates an overall discriminative feature representation for each input video sequence, even when sequence lengths vary greatly, in a feed-forward manner, and simple Euclidean-distance matching can already achieve good re-identification performance. Experiments on the most widely used benchmark datasets show that our method outperforms the state of the art.
